source_text: Χειροτέχνης εἶ; καθεζόμενος ψάλλε· ἀλλ' οὐ βούλει τῷ στόματι ψάλλειν; τῇ διανοίᾳ τοῦτο ποίει· μέγας συνόμιλος ὁ ψαλμός. Οὐδὲν ἐντεῦθεν ὑποστήσῃ δεινὸν, ἀλλ' ὡς ἐν μοναστηρίῳ ἐν τῷ ἐργαστηρίῳ δυνήσῃ καθέζεσθαι· οὐ γὰρ τόπων ἐπιτηδειότης, ἀλλὰ τρόπων ἀκρίβεια τὴν ἡσυχίαν ἡμῖν παρέξεται. Παῦλος γοῦν ἐν ἐργαστηρίῳ τῇ τέχνῃ κεχρημένος, οὐδὲν εἰς τὴν οἰκείαν ἀρετὴν παρεβλάβη. Μὴ τοίνυν λέγε σύ· Πῶς δυνήσομαι χειροτέχνης ὢν καὶ πένης φιλοσοφεῖν; Διὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν μάλιστα δυνήσῃ φιλοσοφεῖν. Καὶ γὰρ πενία πλούτου, καὶ ἐργασία ἀργίας πρὸς εὐλάβειαν ἡμῖν ἐπιτηδειότερον, ὡς ὅ γε πλοῦτος τοῖς μὴ προσέχουσι καὶ ἐμπόδιον γίνεται. Ὅταν γὰρ ὀργὴν δέῃ ἀφεῖναι, ὅταν σβέσαι φθόνον, ὅταν χαλᾶσαι θυμὸν, ὅταν εὐχὴν ἐπιδείξασθαι, ὅταν ἐπιείκειαν καὶ πραότητα, ὅταν φιλοφροσύνην καὶ ἀγάπην, ποῦ γένοιτ' ἂν κώλυμα ἡ πενία; Οὐ γὰρ ἀργύριον καταβαλόντας ταῦτα ἀνύσαι ἔστιν, ἀλλὰ προαίρεσιν ὀρθὴν ἐπιδειξαμένους. Ἐλεημοσύνη μάλιστά ἐστιν ἡ χρημάτων δεομένη, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὴ διὰ τῆς πενίας μειζόνως ἐξέλαμψε· καὶ γὰρ ἡ τοὺς δύο ὀβολοὺς καταβαλοῦσα, ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων ἦν πενεστέρα, καὶ πάντας ὑπερηκόντισε. Μὴ τοίνυν μέγα τι νομίζωμεν εἶναι πλοῦτον, μηδὲ πηλοῦ βελτίονα εἶναι τὸν χρυσὸν λογιζώμεθα· ἡ γὰρ τιμὴ τῆς ὕλης οὐκ ἀπὸ τῆς φύσεως, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς ἡμετέρας διανοίας ἐστίν. Εἰ γάρ τις ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάσειε, πολὺ τοῦ χρυσοῦ σίδηρος ἀναγκαιότερος· ὁ μὲν γὰρ εἰς τὸν βίον οὐδεμίαν εἰσάγει χρείαν, οὗτος δὲ τὸ πλέον ἡμῖν κατεσκεύασε τῆς χρείας μυρίαις τέχναις ὑπηρετούμενος. Καὶ τί λέγω χρυσοῦ καὶ σιδήρου σύγκρισιν; τῶν γὰρ πολυτελῶν λίθων ἀναγκαιότεροι οἱ λίθοι οὗτοι· ἐξ ἐκείνων μὲν γὰρ οὐδὲν ἂν γένοιτο χρηστὸν, ἀπὸ δὲ τούτων οἰκίαι τε καὶ τείχη καὶ πόλεις ἔστησαν. Σὺ δέ μοι δεῖξον, τί τὸ κέρδος ἀπὸ τῶν μαργαριτῶν γένοιτ' ἂν τούτων, μᾶλλον δὲ ποῖον οὐκ ἂν γένοιτο βλάβος; Καὶ γὰρ ἵνα σὺ κόκκον ἕνα φορέσῃς, μυρίοι τῷ λιμῷ πένητες ἄγχονται· ποίας οὖν ἀπολογίας τεύξῃ; τίνος συγγνώμης; Βούλει κοσμῆσαι τὸ πρόσωπον; μὴ μαργαρίταις, ἀλλὰ σωφροσύνῃ καὶ σεμνότητι· οὕτω χαριεστέραν ὄψεται τὴν ὄψιν ὁ ἀνήρ. Ἐκεῖνος μὲν γὰρ ὁ κόσμος καὶ εἰς ζηλοτυπίας ὑποψίαν ἐμβάλλειν εἴωθεν καὶ εἰς ἔχθρας καὶ φιλονεικίας καὶ μάχας· οὐδὲν γὰρ ὄψεως, ὑποπτευομένης ἀηδέστερον· ὁ δὲ τῆς ἐλεημοσύνης καὶ σωφροσύνης κόσμος πᾶσαν μὲν ἐκβάλλει πονηρὰν ὑπόνοιαν, παντὸς δὲ δεσμοῦ σφοδρότερον ἐπισπάσεται τὸν σύνοικον. Οὐ γὰρ οὕτω κάλλους φύσις εὔμορφον ποιεῖ γίνεσθαι τὴν ὄψιν, ὡς ἡ τοῦ θεωροῦντος αὐτὴν διάθεσις· διάθεσιν δὲ οὐδὲν οὕτως, ὡς σωφροσύνη καὶ σεμνότης ποιεῖν εἴωθεν. Ὥστε κἂν εὔμορφος ᾖ τις, ἀπεχθῶς δὲ πρὸς αὐτὴν ὁ ἀνὴρ ἔχῃ, πάντων αἰσχροτέρα αὐτῷ φανεῖται· κἂν μὴ τύχῃ τις εὐπρεπὴς οὖσα, ἡδέως δὲ πρὸς αὐτὴν ὁ ἀνὴρ ἔχῃ, πάντων εὐμορφοτέρα αὐτῷ φανεῖται· οὐ γὰρ ἐν τῇ φύσει τῶν ὁρωμένων, ἀλλ' ἐν τῇ διαθέσει τῶν ὁρώντων αἱ ψῆφοι γίνονται. Καλλώπισον τοίνυν τὴν ὄψιν σωφροσύνῃ, σεμνότητι, ἐλεημοσύνῃ, φιλανθρωπίᾳ, ἀγάπῃ, τῇ περὶ τὸν ἄνδρα φιλοφροσύνῃ, ἐπιεικείᾳ, πραότητι, ἀνεξικακίᾳ· ταῦτα τῆς ἀρετῆς τὰ χρώματα· διὰ τούτων ἀγγέλους, οὐκ ἀνθρώπους ἐραστὰς ἐπισπάσῃ, διὰ τούτων αὐτὸν ἔχεις τὸν Θεὸν ἐπαινέτην· ὅταν δὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἀποδέξηται, καὶ τὸν ἄνδρα σοι ὑποτάξει πάντως.
thought_title: Poverty and virtue adorn the face better than pearls
orientation: Chrysostom is addressing the catechumens about reforming their habits, and has just urged them to bridle the tongue; now he turns to the poor artisan and to women's adornment.
pass_a_gloss: Are you a craftsman? Sitting, sing psalms. But you do not wish to sing psalms with the mouth? Do this with the mind. A great companion is the psalm. You will undergo nothing terrible from this, but as in a monastery you will be able to sit in the workshop. For not suitability of places, but strictness of habits will provide us the quiet. Paul at any rate, using his craft in a workshop, was harmed in nothing with respect to his own virtue. Do not then say: How will I be able, being a craftsman and poor, to practice philosophy? For this reason indeed most of all you will be able to practice philosophy. For poverty than wealth, and work than idleness, is more suitable for us toward piety, just as wealth at least becomes also a hindrance to those not paying attention. For whenever it is necessary to let go of anger, whenever to quench envy, whenever to relax rage, whenever to display prayer, whenever gentleness and meekness, whenever friendliness and love, where would poverty become a hindrance? For it is not possible to accomplish these things by paying down silver, but by displaying right choice. Almsgiving most of all is the thing needing money, but this too through poverty shone more greatly. For also the woman who put in the two obols was poorer than all people, and surpassed all. Let us not then consider wealth to be something great, nor let us reckon gold to be better than clay. For the honor of the material is not from the nature, but from our thinking. For if someone should examine precisely, iron is much more necessary than gold. For the one introduces no need into life, but this one has furnished for us the greater part of need, serving with countless crafts. And why do I speak of a comparison of gold and iron? For these stones are more necessary than the costly stones. For from those nothing useful would come, but from these houses and walls and cities have stood. But you show me, what would be the gain from these pearls, or rather what harm would not come? For in order that you may wear one grain, countless poor are strangled by famine. Of what defense then will you obtain? Of what pardon? Do you wish to adorn the face? Not with pearls, but with self-control and dignity. Thus the husband will see the face as more graceful. For that adornment is accustomed to cast also into suspicion of jealousy and into enmities and quarrels and fights. For nothing is more unpleasant than a face that is suspected. But the adornment of almsgiving and self-control casts out every wicked suspicion, and will draw the husband more strongly than every bond. For not so much does the nature of beauty make the face become shapely, as the disposition of the one beholding it. And nothing is accustomed to make disposition so much as self-control and dignity. So that even if someone is shapely, but the husband is hostilely disposed toward her, she will appear to him uglier than all. And even if someone happens not to be comely, but the husband is sweetly disposed toward her, she will appear to him more shapely than all. For not in the nature of the things seen, but in the disposition of those seeing, the votes are cast. Adorn then the face with self-control, dignity, almsgiving, love of humanity, love, friendliness toward the husband, gentleness, meekness, forbearance. These are the colors of virtue. Through these you will draw angels, not human lovers. Through these you have God himself as praiser. And whenever God accepts, he will subject the husband to you entirely.

choices.why: The verb means to sing psalms or sacred songs, not merely to sing generally; the context is the craftsman's private devotion.
Chrysostom uses the verb in the ascetic sense of living a disciplined, virtuous life, not academic philosophy.
In this context of women's adornment, σωφροσύνη denotes chastity and moderation, rendered as self-control to cover the moral sense.
Σεμνότης here is the gravity and honorable bearing that adorns a wife; dignity captures the moral weight.
The compound means bearing wrongs patiently; forbearance is the standard English equivalent.
The verb means to place under authority; in the marital context it means God will make the husband devoted and submissive to her.

bible_refs.note: ἡ τοὺς δύο ὀβολοὺς καταβαλοῦσα refers to the poor widow who put in two lepta (obols).

pass_b_english: Are you a craftsman? Sit at your work and sing psalms. But you do not want to sing psalms with your mouth? Do it with your mind. A psalm is a great companion. You will suffer nothing terrible from this, but you will be able to sit in your workshop as if in a monastery. For it is not the suitability of places but the discipline of our habits that gives us quiet. Paul, at any rate, worked at his trade in a workshop and suffered no harm to his virtue. So do not say, "How will I be able to practice philosophy when I am a craftsman and poor?" For this very reason you will be able to practice philosophy all the more. Poverty is more suited to piety than wealth, and work than idleness, just as wealth becomes a hindrance to those who are not careful. For when you need to let go of anger, to quench envy, to relax your temper, to show prayer, to show gentleness and meekness, to show kindness and love, where could poverty be an obstacle? These things are not accomplished by paying out silver, but by showing a right choice. Almsgiving is the thing that most requires money, but even this shone more brightly through poverty. For the woman who put in two obols was poorer than all people, and she surpassed them all (Mark 12:42). Let us not, then, think wealth is something great, nor consider gold better than clay. For the honor of a material comes not from its nature but from our own thinking. If someone examined carefully, iron is far more necessary than gold. Gold brings no need into life, but iron has furnished most of our needs, serving countless crafts. And why do I compare gold and iron? These ordinary stones are more necessary than precious stones. From those nothing useful could come, but from these houses, walls, and cities have been built. But show me what gain could come from these pearls—or rather, what harm could not come from them? For so that you may wear a single pearl, thousands of poor people are strangled by hunger. What defense will you find then? What pardon? Do you want to adorn your face? Not with pearls, but with self-control and dignity. That is how your husband will see your face as more graceful. That other adornment usually casts suspicion of jealousy, and leads to enmities, quarrels, and fights. For nothing is more unpleasant than a face that is suspected. But the adornment of almsgiving and self-control casts out every evil suspicion and draws your husband to you more powerfully than any bond. For the natural beauty of a face does not make it appear lovely as much as the disposition of the one looking at it does. And nothing creates that disposition as much as self-control and dignity. So even if a woman is beautiful, if her husband is hostile toward her, she will seem uglier than everyone to him. And if a woman happens not to be attractive, but her husband is kindly disposed toward her, she will seem more beautiful than everyone to him. For the judgments are made not in the nature of the things seen, but in the disposition of those who see. Adorn your face, then, with self-control, dignity, almsgiving, love for humanity, love, kindness toward your husband, gentleness, meekness, forbearance. These are the colors of virtue. Through these you will draw angels, not human lovers, to yourself. Through these you have God himself as your admirer. And when God approves, he will certainly subject your husband to you as well.

last_rejected.why: εὐχὴν here means 'vow' not 'prayer'; context is about oaths/vows throughout.
last_rejected.ruling: εὐχὴν commonly means 'prayer'; context lists virtues to display, not vows. 'Prayer' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: For the natural beauty of a face does not make it appear lovely as much as the disposition of the one looking at it does
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ γὰρ οὕτω κάλλους φύσις εὔμορφον ποιεῖ γίνεσθαι τὴν ὄψιν, ὡς ἡ τοῦ θεωροῦντος αὐτὴν διάθεσις
last_rejected.why: κάλλους φύσις is 'the nature of beauty,' not 'natural beauty of a face.' The Greek says 'the nature of beauty' (abstract), not 'natural beauty' (inherent quality). This changes the philosophical point: it's about beauty's nature generally, not about innate vs. acquired beauty.
last_rejected.fix: For the nature of beauty does not make a face appear lovely so much as the disposition of the one looking at it
last_rejected.ruling: κάλλους φύσις = 'nature of beauty'; 'natural beauty' is a reasonable rendering. No meaning change; philosophical point preserved.

last_rejected.quote: And nothing creates that disposition as much as self-control and dignity
last_rejected.source_quote: διάθεσιν δὲ οὐδὲν οὕτως, ὡς σωφροσύνη καὶ σεμνότης ποιεῖν εἴωθεν
last_rejected.why: ποιεῖν εἴωθεν means 'is accustomed to create,' not 'creates.' The habitual aspect is lost, changing the modality from customary to absolute.
last_rejected.fix: And nothing is so accustomed to create that disposition as self-control and dignity
last_rejected.ruling: εἴωθεν adds habitual nuance, but 'creates' conveys core meaning. Minor preference, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: For the judgments are made not in the nature of the things seen, but in the disposition of those who see
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἐν τῇ φύσει τῶν ὁρωμένων, ἀλλ' ἐν τῇ διαθέσει τῶν ὁρώντων αἱ ψῆφοι γίνονται
last_rejected.why: ψῆφοι means 'votes' or 'verdicts,' not 'judgments.' The metaphor is of voting/pebbles used for voting. 'Judgments' loses the specific metaphor. But is this major? 'Judgments' captures the sense. Not reporting.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter self-reports as not reporting; 'judgments' captures sense of ψῆφοι adequately.

last_rejected.quote: Through these you have God himself as your admirer
last_rejected.source_quote: διὰ τούτων αὐτὸν ἔχεις τὸν Θεὸν ἐπαινέτην
last_rejected.why: ἐπαινέτην means 'praiser' or 'one who praises,' not 'admirer.' 'Admirer' suggests romantic or aesthetic appreciation; 'praiser' or 'one who commends' is the religious sense intended. This changes the theological register.
last_rejected.fix: Through these you have God himself as your praiser
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπαινέτης = 'praiser'; 'admirer' is within range. No meaning change or theological distortion; context is clear.
